title: Dialects and neighbors: one language, many voices
goal: Recognize the main regional accents of Sweden and Finland-Swedish, and read simple Norwegian and Danish with the help of a handful of sound correspondences.
bekal: you can recognize skånska, göteborgska, norrländska, gotländska and Finland-Swedish by two or three key features each
you can use spelling correspondences to read a Norwegian or Danish email
you can steer around the classic false friends between the Scandinavian languages
wave: Go back to Unit 14: reread the slang list (asså, typ, ba, fett, schysst) and sort each word into "I'd say it to friends" or "I only need to recognize it" — then read lines 6–7 of today's first dialogue aloud twice, once with a flat Finland-Swedish melody and once with a singing Stockholm one.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Morjens!
dialogs.intro: Dian's first week at her new job at a sustainability consultancy in Stockholm — including a day trip to a client in Luleå, far up north. Back in the office, over lunch in the staff kitchen she meets Mikaela, who has just moved over from Vasa on Finland's west coast — and the talk soon turns to how differently Swedish can sound.

lines.speaker: Mikaela:
lines.text: Morjens! Du måste vara Dian. Jag heter Mikaela, jag började också i måndags.
lines.id: Hi there! You must be Dian. I'm Mikaela — I started on Monday too.

notes: **Morjens** (**MOR-yens**) is the everyday Finland-Swedish "hi", alongside *moi*, borrowed straight from Finnish. Swedish is one of Finland's two national languages, spoken as a first language by roughly 5 percent of the population — mainly along the south and west coasts (Helsingfors, Åbo, Vasa) and on Åland. Notice that Swedish has its own names for these cities: *Helsingfors* = Helsinki, *Åbo* = Turku, *Vasa* = Vaasa.

**Rikssvenska** (**RIKS-sven-skah**) is the standard Swedish of Sweden, and **rikssvenskar** is what Finland-Swedes call Swedes from Sweden. In Sweden itself the word mostly means "standard Swedish" as opposed to dialect. **Joo** (yeah) is another Finnish loan that you will hear in every Finland-Swedish conversation.

**Vi har inga tonaccenter** — Mikaela is right: Finland-Swedish has no word tones. The pair *anden* (the duck, tone 1) and *anden* (the spirit, tone 2) sounds the same in Helsinki. Add short, crisp consonants and vowels that stay close to the spelling, and you get the reason many learners find Finland-Swedish the easiest variety of all to follow.

**Gött** (**yöt**) is the West Swedish word for "nice, lovely, good" — a meal, a sauna, a lazy Sunday can all be *gött*. Standard Swedish has *gott* (tasty) and *skönt* (comfortable), but *gött* has spread far beyond Göteborg through TV and music. **Kiva** is its Finland-Swedish counterpart, from Finnish.

**Henne förstod jag knappt** — the object *henne* is fronted for contrast (Unit 1: the fundament takes what you want to highlight). The verb stays second and the subject moves behind it. **Knappt** (**knahpt**) means "barely, hardly" and sits in the sentence-adverb slot, just like *inte*. **Int** is the northern (and Finland-Swedish) short form of *inte*, and **i varannan mening** means "in every other sentence".

**Hjälpas åt** (**YEL-pahs oht**) means "to help each other, to pitch in together". It is a particle verb with a reciprocal *-s* (recall *vi ses*, *vi hörs*). **Man vänjer sig** (**mahn VEN-yer say**) — "you get used to it" — uses the generic *man* with a reflexive verb: *vänja sig vid något*, to get used to something.

grammars.title: Telling the regions apart
body: Nobody expects you to speak a dialect, but at B2 you should recognize where a speaker roughly comes from — and not panic when the melody changes. Listen for these features first.

head: Region
What you will notice
A word you may hear
rows: the basis of standard Swedish; strong two-tone melody; younger speakers open *ä* before *r* (*här*, *där*)
a back, throaty *r* like French or German; long vowels glide into diphthongs; a slower, rounder melody
fast, sing-song rhythm; a love of puns (*göteborgsvitsar*); many local words
clipped, short words; a flatter melody; *jo* and *nä* everywhere
diphthongs where standard Swedish has plain long vowels; a rising, almost questioning melody
no word tones; crisp consonants; vowels close to the spelling; Finnish loanwords

after: Dialect in Sweden carries less social stigma than in many countries. Newsreaders, politicians and professors often keep a clear regional accent, and a Skåne or Norrland voice on national radio is completely normal.

Two accents to keep apart: **dialekt** is a regional variety spoken by native speakers; **brytning** is the accent of someone who learned Swedish as a second language (*hon pratar svenska med lätt brytning*). Your own accent is a *brytning* — and that is fine.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Skandinaviskt videomöte
dialogs.intro: A week later. Dian and Mikaela sit in a meeting room in Stockholm; on the screen are Ingrid from the Oslo office and Mads from Copenhagen. Everybody speaks their own language. Ingrid's lines are Norwegian, Mads's lines Danish.

notes: **Skandinaviska** is what Nordic colleagues call the habit of each speaking their own language and adjusting a little: slower tempo, fewer local words, no slang. Linguists call the three languages **grannspråk** ("neighbor languages"). Switching to English is common too, especially with young Danes — but suggesting *skandinaviska* first is seen as a friendly gesture.

**Rolig** is the most famous false friend in the North: Swedish *rolig* = fun, funny; Danish and Norwegian *rolig* = calm, quiet. *Tag det roligt* is the Danish twin of Swedish *ta det lugnt*. **Rar** splits three ways: Swedish "sweet, kind", Danish "nice, kind", Norwegian "strange, odd".

**Flink** is a three-way trap as well: Danish *flink* = kind, nice; Norwegian *flink* = clever, good at something; Swedish *flink* = quick, nimble (*flinka fingrar*). When a Norwegian says *du er flink!*, take it as a compliment on your skills.

**Danish pronunciation** is the hard part, not the spelling. Danes swallow many consonants (the *d* in *mad* sounds almost like English "th" in "the"), and use a glottal catch called *stød*. Read Danish on paper first and you will understand far more than by ear. Norwegian is the reverse: it **sounds** close to Swedish but **looks** close to Danish.

**Köra på** literally "drive on" is colloquial for "go with, go for": *Vi kör på det!* (Let's go with that!). **Allihop** (**AHL-lee-hoop**) = all of you, everybody — a warmer, more spoken word than *alla*.

**Komma överens** (**KOM-mah Ö-ver-ens**) = to agree, reach agreement. The perfect *vi har kommit överens* is the classic way of closing a negotiation point. Compare *hålla med* (Unit 8), which means to agree with someone's opinion.

grammars.title: Reading Norwegian and Danish with Swedish eyes
body: Norwegian (bokmål) and Danish share most of their spelling, and both differ from Swedish in regular, predictable ways. Learn these correspondences and a Norwegian newspaper becomes about 80 percent readable.

head: Swedish
Norwegian
Danish
Pattern
rows: Danish softens *t, k, p* → *d, g, b*
Norwegian *å* for Swedish *u* in some words

after: Definite forms work just as in Swedish: Norwegian *gaten*, Danish *gaden* = Swedish *gatan*. Danish has no *-a* ending, so *flaskan* becomes *flasken*.

The real obstacle is everyday vocabulary that differs completely: *pratar* = Norwegian *snakker*, Danish *snakker*; *flicka* = Norwegian *jente*, Danish *pige*; *byxor* = Norwegian *bukser*, Danish *bukser*. When a word makes no sense, try the context before the dictionary.

blocks.text: The *frokost* trap is a real one for business trips: invited to *frokost* in Copenhagen, you should turn up around noon, not at eight in the morning. Danes call breakfast *morgenmad*. And if a Danish friend *griner* at your joke, be pleased — they are laughing, not crying.

blocks.title: Surviving a Scandinavian meeting
items: Speak your own language a little slower than usual, and drop slang and very local words.
Use international or shared words when you can: *ett projekt*, *en budget*, *en deadline* are understood everywhere.
Check understanding openly — it is not rude: *Hängde ni med?* (Did you follow?), *Ska jag ta det på engelska?*
Write numbers and dates in the chat. Danish counting (*halvtreds* = 50) defeats most Swedes too.

blocks.text: Words like these are called **finlandismer** (finlandisms). They are correct, standard Finland-Swedish — not mistakes — and the Swedish Language Council in Finland even recommends some of them. Most Finland-Swedes switch effortlessly to Sweden-Swedish words when they live in Stockholm, as Mikaela slowly will.

Inside Finland-Swedish there is huge variety. The dialects of Ostrobothnia around Vasa (*österbottniska*) can be hard even for people from Helsingfors, while the Swedish of Åland sounds closer to the dialects of the Stockholm archipelago just across the water.

blocks.title: Spiral review — back to Unit 1
items: Rewrite three dialogue lines of this unit with a different fundament: *Jag förstod henne knappt* → *Henne förstod jag knappt* → *Knappt förstod jag henne* (very emphatic).
Say which version you would use to contrast her with someone else, and which is neutral.
Remember: whatever you front, the finite verb stays in second place.
